entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Isa 26:1</reference> <div eID="gen13140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13141" type="x-p"/> Thus the second hymnic echo has its confirmation in a prophecy against Moab, on the basis of which a third hymnic echo now arises. Whilst on the other side, in the land of Moab, the people are trodden down, and its lofty castles demolished, the people in the land of Judah can boast of an impregnable city. <hi type="italic">“In that day will this song be sung in the land of Judah: A city of defence is ours; salvation He sets for walls and bulwark.”</hi> According to the punctuation, this ought to be rendered, “A city is a shelter for us;” but עז עיר seem rather to be connected, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.17.19">Pro 17:19</reference>, “a city of strong, i.e., of impregnable offence and defence.” The subject of ישׁית is Jehovah. The figure indicates what He is constantly doing, and ever doing afresh; for the walls and bulwarks of Jerusalem (<hi type="italic">chēl</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">Lam 2:8</reference>, the small outside wall which encloses all the fortifications) are not dead stone, but <hi type="italic">yeshuâh</hi>, ever living and never exhausted <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.18">Isa 60:18</reference>). In just the same sense Jehovah is called elsewhere the wall of Jerusalem, and even a wall of fire in Zec 2:9 - parallels which show that <hi type="italic">yeshuâh</hi> is intended to be taken as the accusative of the object, and not as the accusative of the predicate, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Isa 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.7">Psa 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.7">Psa 84:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6">Jer 22:6</reference> (Luzzatto).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.2">Isa 26:2</reference> <div eID="gen13141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13142" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Isa 26:1</reference> this city is thought of as still empty: for, like paradise, in which man was placed, it is first of all a creation of God; and hence the exclamation in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.2">Isa 26:2</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Open ye the gates, that a righteous people may enter, one keeping truthfulness.”</hi> The cry is a heavenly one; and those who open, if indeed we are at liberty to inquire who they are, must be angels. We recall to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference>, but the scene is a different one. The author of Ps 118 has given individuality to this passage in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.19">Psa 118:19</reference>, Psa 118:20. <hi type="italic">Goi tzaddik</hi> (a righteous nation) is the church of the righteous, as in Isa 24:16. <hi type="italic">Goi</hi> (nation) is used here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>, with reference to Israel, which has now by grace become a righteous nation, and has been established in covenant truth towards God, who keepeth truth (<hi type="italic">'emunim</hi>, from <hi type="italic">'ēmūn</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.24">Psa 31:24</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference> <div eID="gen13142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13143" type="x-p"/> The relation of Israel and Jehovah to one another is now a permanent one. <hi type="italic">“Thou keepest the firmly-established mind in peace, peace; for his confidence rests on Thee.”</hi> A gnome (borrowed in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.7-Ps.112.8">Psa 112:7-8</reference>), but in a lyrical connection, and with a distinct reference to the church of the last days. There is no necessity to take סמוּ יצר as standing for יצר סמוּך, as Knobel does. The state of mind is mentioned here as designating the person possessing it, according to his inmost nature. יצר (the mind) is the whole attitude and habit of a man as inwardly constituted, i.e., as a being capable of thought and will. סמוּך is the same, regarded as having a firm hold in itself, and this it has whenever it has a firm hold on God (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference>). This is the mind of the new Israel, and Jehovah keeps it, <hi type="italic">shâlom</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâlom</hi> (peace, peace; accusative predicates, used in the place of a consequential clause), i.e., so that deep and constant peace abides therein (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Phi 4:7</reference>). Such a mind is thus kept by Jehovah, because its trust is placed in Jehovah. בּטוּח refers to יצר, according to Ewald, §149, <hi type="italic">d</hi>, and is therefore equivalent to הוּא בּטוּח (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">Psa 55:20</reference>), the passive participle, like the Latin <hi type="italic">confisus</hi>, <hi type="italic">fretus</hi>. To hang on God, or to be thoroughly devoted to Him, secures both stability and peace.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Isa 26:4</reference> <div eID="gen13143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13144" type="x-p"/> A cry goes forth again, as if from heaven, exhorting Israel to continue in this mind. <hi type="italic">“Hang confidently on Jehovah for ever: for in Jah, Jehovah, is an everlasting rock.”</hi> The combination <hi type="italic">Jah Jehovah</hi> is only met with here and in Isa 12:2. It is the proper name of God the Redeemer in the most emphatic form. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">essentiae</hi> frequently stands before the predicate (Ges. §151, 3); here, however, it stands before the subject, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.5">Psa 78:5</reference>; Psa 55:19. In Jah Jehovah (<hi type="italic">munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">tzakeph</hi>) there is an everlasting rock, i.e., He is essentially such a rock (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deu 32:4</reference>, like <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference> for <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">Isa 12:2</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5-Isa.26.6">Isa 26:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen13144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13145" type="x-p"/> He has already proved Himself to be such a rock, on which everything breaks that would attack the faithful whom He surrounds. <hi type="italic">“For He hath bent down them that dwell on high; the towering castle, He tore it down, tore it down to the earth, cast it into dust. The foot treads it to pieces, feet of the poor, steps of the lowly.”</hi> Passing beyond the fall of Moab, the fall of the imperial city is celebrated, to which Moab was only an annex (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.2">Isa 25:1-2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.10-Isa.24.12">Isa 24:10-12</reference>). The futures are determined by the preterite; and the <hi type="italic">anadiplosis</hi>, which in other instances (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1">Isa 25:1</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.118.11">Psa 118:11</reference>) links together derivatives or variations of form, is satisfied in this instance with changing the forms of the suffix. The second thought of <reference osisRef="Isa.26.6">Isa 26:6</reference> is a more emphatic repetition of the first: it is trodden down; the oppression of those who have been hitherto oppressed is trodden down.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">Isa 26:7</reference> <div eID="gen13145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13146" type="x-p"/> The righteous, who go astray according to the judgment of the world, thus arrive at a goal from which their way appears in a very different light. <hi type="italic">“The path that the righteous man takes is smoothness; Thou makest the course of the righteous smooth.”</hi> ישׁר is an accusative predicate: Thou rollest it, i.e., Thou smoothest it, so that it is just as if it had been bevelled with a rule, and leads quite straight (on the derivative <hi type="italic">peles</hi>, a level, see at <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference>) and without interruption to the desired end. The song has here fallen into the language of a <hi type="italic">mashal</hi> of Solomon (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">Pro 4:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.6">Pro 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Pro 5:21</reference>). It pauses here to reflect, as if at the close of a strophe.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.8-Isa.26.9">Isa 26:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen13146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13147" type="x-p"/> It then commences again in a lyrical tone in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.8">Isa 26:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> : <hi type="italic">“We have also waited for Thee, that Thou shouldest come in the path of Thy judgments; the desire of the soul went after Thy name, and after Thy remembrance. With my soul I desired Thee in the night; yea, with my spirit deep within me, I longed to have Thee here: for when Thy judgments strike the earth, the inhabitants of the earth learn righteousness.”</hi> In the opinion of Hitzig, Knobel, Drechsler, and others, the prophet here comes back from the ideal to the actual present. But this is not the case. The church of the last days, looking back to the past, declares with what longing it has waited for that manifestation of the righteousness of God which has now taken place. “The path of Thy judgments:” <hi type="italic">'orach mishpâtēkâ</hi> belongs to the <hi type="italic">te</hi>; <hi type="italic">venientem</hi> (or <hi type="italic">venturum</hi>) being understood. The clause follows the poetical construction ארח בּוא, after the analogy of דרך הלך. They longed for God to come as a Redeemer in the way of His judgments. The “name” and “remembrance” ad the nature of God, that has become nameable and memorable through self-assertion and self-manifestation (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Exo 3:15</reference>). They desired that God should present Himself again to the consciousness and memory of man, by such an act as should break through His concealment and silence. The prophet says this more especially of himself; for he feels himself “in spirit” to be a member of the perfected church. “My soul” and “my spirit” are accusatives giving a more precise definition (Ewald, §281,<hi type="italic">c</hi>). “<hi type="italic">The night</hi>” is the night of affliction, as in Isa 21:11. In connection with this, the word <hi type="italic">shichēr</hi> (lit. to dig for a thing, to seek it eagerly) is employed here, with a play upon <hi type="italic">shachar</hi>. The dawning of the morning after a night of suffering was the object for which he longed, <hi type="italic">naphshi</hi> (my soul), i.e., with his entire personality (<hi type="italic">Pyschol</hi>. p. 202), and <hi type="italic">ruchi b'kirbi</hi> (my spirit within me), i.e., with the spirit of his mind, πνεῦμα τοῦ νοός (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 183). And why? Because, as often as God manifested Himself in judgment, this brought men to the knowledge, and possibly also to the recognition, of what was right (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Will learn:</hi>” <hi type="italic">lâmdu</hi> is a <hi type="italic">praet. gnomicum</hi>, giving the result of much practical experience.

Jehovah, Thou wilt establish peace for us: for Thou hast accomplished all our work for us. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference> <div eID="gen13149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13150" type="x-p"/> The tyrants who usurped the rule over Israel have now utterly disappeared. <hi type="italic">“Dead men live not again, shades do not rise again: so hast Thou visited and destroyed them, and caused all their memory to perish.”</hi> The meaning is not that Jehovah had put them to death because there was no resurrection at all after death; for, as we shall see further on, the prophet was acquainted with such a resurrection. In <hi type="italic">mēthim</hi> (dead men) and <hi type="italic">rephâ'im</hi> (shades) he had directly in mind the oppressors of Israel, who had been thrust down into the region of the shades (like the king of Babylon in chapter 14), so that there was no possibility of their being raised up or setting themselves up again. The לכן is not argumentative (which would be very freezing in this highly lyrical connection), but introduces what must have occurred <hi type="italic">eo ipso</hi> when the other had taken place (it corresponds to the Greek ἄρα, and is used here in the same way as in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">Jer 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.33">Jer 2:33</reference>; Zec 11:7; <reference osisRef="Job.34.25">Job 34:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>). They had fallen irrevocably into Sheol (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Psa 49:15</reference>), and consequently God had swept them away, so that not even their name was perpetuated.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference> <div eID="gen13150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13151" type="x-p"/> Israel, when it has such cause as this for praising Jehovah, will have become a numerous people once more. <hi type="italic">“Thou hast added to the nation, O Jehovah, hast added to the nation; glorified Thyself; moved out all the borders of the land.”</hi> The verb יסף, which is construed in other cases with על, אל ,, here with ל, carried its object within itself: to add, i.e., to give an increase. The allusion is to the same thing as that which caused the prophet to rejoice in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.19-Isa.49.20">Isa 49:19-20</reference>; Isa 54:1., Mic 2:12; Mic 4:7; Oba 1:19-20, and many other passages; and for <hi type="italic">richaktâ</hi>, more especially Mic 7:11). Just as <reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Isa 26:13</reference> recals the bondage in Egypt, and <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference> the destruction of Pharaoh in the Red Sea, so <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Isa 26:16</reference> recals the numerical strength of the nation, and the extent of the country in the time of David and Solomon. At the same time, we cannot say that the prophet intended to recall these to mind. The antitypical relation, in which the last times stand to these events and circumstances of the past, is a fact in sacred history, though not particularly referred to here.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16-Isa.26.18">Isa 26:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen13151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13152" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">tephillâh</hi> now returns to the retrospective glance already cast in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.8">Isa 26:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> into that night of affliction, which preceded the redemption that had come. <hi type="italic">“Jehovah, in trouble they missed Thee, poured out light supplication when Thy chastisement came upon them. As a woman with child, who draws near to her delivery, writhes and cries out in her pangs, so were we in Thy sight, O Jehovah. We went with child, we writhed; it was as if we brought forth wind. We brought no deliverance to the land, and the inhabitants of the world did not come to the light.”</hi> The substantive circumstantial clause in the parallel line, למו מוּסר, <hi type="italic">castigatione</hi> <hi type="italic">tua</hi> <hi type="italic">eos</hi> <hi type="italic">affilgente</hi> (ל as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference>), corresponds to בּצּר; and לחשׁ צקוּן, a preterite עצוּק etire = יצק, <reference osisRef="Job.28.2">Job 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference>, to be poured out and melt away) with <hi type="italic">Nun</hi> <hi type="italic">paragogic</hi> (which is only met with again in <reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">Deu 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.16">Deu 8:16</reference>, the <hi type="italic">yekōshūn</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa 29:21</reference> being, according to the syntax, the future of <hi type="italic">kōsh</hi>), answers to <hi type="italic">pâkad</hi>, which is used here as in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.15">1Sa 25:15</reference>, in the sense of <hi type="italic">lustrando desiderare</hi>. <hi type="italic">Lachash</hi> is a quiet, whispering prayer (like the whispering of forms of incantation in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.3">Isa 3:3</reference>); sorrow renders speechless in the long run; and a consciousness of sin crushes so completely, that a man does not dare to address God aloud (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Isa 29:4</reference>). Pregnancy and pangs are symbols of a state of expectation strained to the utmost, the object of which appears all the closer the more the pains increase. Often, says the perfected church, as it looks back upon its past history, often did we regard the coming of salvation as certain; but again and again were our hopes deceived. The first כּמו is equivalent to כּ, “as a woman with child,” etc. (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">Isa 8:22</reference>); the second is equivalent to כּאשׁר, “as it were, we brought forth wind.” This is not an inverted expression, signifying we brought forth as it were wind; but כמו governs the whole sentence in the sense of “(it was) <hi type="italic">as if</hi>.” The issue of all their painful toil was like the result of a false pregnancy (<hi type="italic">empneumatosis</hi>), a delivery of wind. This state of things also proceeded from Jehovah, as the expression “before Thee” implies. It was a consequence of the sins of Israel, and of a continued want of true susceptibility to the blessings of salvation. Side by side with their disappointed hope, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.18">Isa 26:18</reference> places the ineffectual character of their won efforts. Israel’s own doings - no, they could never make the land into ישׁוּעת (i.e., bring it into a state of complete salvation); and (so might the final clause be understood) they waited in vain for the judgment of Jehovah upon the sinful world that was at enmity against them, or they made ineffectual efforts to overcome it. This explanation is favoured by the fact, that throughout the whole of this cycle of prophecies <hi type="italic">yōshbē tēbēl</hi> does not mean the inhabitants of the holy land, but of the globe at large in the sense of “the world” (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.5-Isa.24.6">Isa 24:5-6</reference>). Again, the relation of יפּלוּ to the תּפּיל in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>, land the figure previously employed of the pains of child-birth, speak most strongly in favour of the conclusion, that <hi type="italic">nâphal</hi> is here used for the falling of the fruit of the womb (cf., Wis. 7:3, <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. xix. 110, καταπεσεῖν and πεσεῖν). And <hi type="italic">yōshbē</hi> <hi type="italic">tēbēl</hi> (the inhabitants of the world) fits in with this sense (viz., that the expected increase of the population never came), from the fact that in this instance the reference is not to <hi type="italic">the</hi> inhabitants of the earth; but the words signify inhabitants generally, or, as we should say, young, new-born “mortals.” The punishment of the land under the weight of the empire still continued, and a new generation did not come to the light of day to populate the desolate land (cf., <hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 414).

Instead of singing what has occurred, the tephillah places itself in the midst of the occurrence itself. <hi type="italic">“Thy dead will live, my corpses rise again. Awake and rejoice, ye that lie in the dust! For thy dew is dew of the lights, and the earth will bring shades to the day.”</hi> The prophet speaks thus out of the heart of the church of the last times. In consequence of the long-continued sufferings and chastisements, it has been melted down to a very small remnant; and many of those whom it could once truly reckon as its own, are now lying as corpses in the dust of the grave. The church, filled with hope which will not be put to shame, now calls to itself, “Thy dead will live” (מתיך יחיוּ, reviviscent, as in המּתים תּסהיּת, the resurrection of the dead), and consoles itself with the working of divine grace ad power, which is even now setting itself in motion: “my corpses will rise again” (יקמוּן נבלתי, <hi type="italic">nebēlah</hi>: a word without a plural, but frequently used in a plural sense, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>, and therefore connected with יקמוּן, equivalent to תקמנה: here before a light suffix, with the <hi type="italic">ê</hi> retained, which is lost in other cases). The plural implies that there is a perfect fulness of the lights of life in God (“the Father of lights,” Jam 1:17). Out of these there is born the gentle dew, which gives new life to the bones that have been sown in the ground (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>) - a figure full of mystery, which is quite needlessly wiped away by Hofmann’s explanation, viz., that it is equivalent to <hi type="italic">tal hōrōth</hi>, “dew of thorough saturating.” Luther, who renders it, “Thy dew is a dew of the green field,” stands alone among the earlier translators. The Targum, Syriac, Vulgate, and Saad. all render it, “Thy dew is light dew;” and with the uniform connection in which the Scriptures place <hi type="italic">'or</hi> (light) and <hi type="italic">chayyı̄m</hi> (life), this rendering is natural enough. We now translate still further, “and the earth (<hi type="italic">vâ'âretz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Pro 25:3</reference>, whereas וארץ is almost always in the construct state) will bring shades to the day” (<hi type="italic">hippil</hi>, as a causative of <hi type="italic">nâphal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.18">Isa 26:18</reference>), i.e., bring forth again the dead that have sunken into it (like Luther’s rendering, “and the land will cast out the dead” - the rendering of our English version also: Tr.). The dew from the glory of God falls like a heavenly seed into the bosom of the earth; and in consequence of this, the earth gives out from itself the shades which have hitherto been held fast beneath the ground, so that they appear alive again on the surface of the earth. Those who understand <reference osisRef="Isa.26.18">Isa 26:18</reference> as relating to the earnestly descried overthrow of the lords of the world, interpret this passage accordingly, as meaning either, “and thou castest down shades to the earth” (ארץ, <hi type="italic">acc. loci,</hi> = עד־ארץ, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5">Isa 26:5</reference>, לארץ, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.12">Isa 25:12</reference>), or, “and the earth causeth shades to fall,” i.e., to fall into itself. When compared with the New Testament Apocalypse, it is “the first resurrection” which is here predicted by Isaiah. The church of the period of glory on this side is a church of those who have been miraculously saved and wakened up from the dead. Their persecutors lie at their feet beneath the ground.

Instead of the dual דּלתיך (as the house-door is called, though not the chamber-door), the word is pointed דּלת (from דּלה = דּלת), just as the prophet intentionally chooses the feminine חבי instead of חבה. The nation is thought of as feminine in this particular instance (cf., Isa 54:7-8 ); because Jehovah, its avenger and protector, is acting on its behalf, whilst in a purely passive attitude it hides itself in Him. Just as Noah, behind whom Jehovah shut the door of the ark, was hidden in the ark whilst the water-floods of the judgment poured down without, so should the church be shut off from the world without in its life of prayer, because a judgment of Jehovah was at hand. “He goeth out of His place” (verbatim the same as in Mic 1:3), i.e., not out of His own divine life, as it rests within Himself, but out of the sphere of the manifested glory in which He presents Himself to the spirits. He goeth forth thence equipped for judgment, to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth upon him (the singular used collectively), and more especially their blood-guiltiness. The prohibition of murder was given to the sons of Noah, and therefore was one of the stipulations of “the covenant of old” ( Isa 24:5 ). The earth supplies two witnesses: (1.) the innocent blood which has been violently shed (on dâmim , see Isa 1:15 ), which she has had to suck up, and which is now exposed, and cries for vengeance; and (2.) the persons themselves who have been murdered in their innocence, and who are slumbering within her. Streams of blood come to light and bear testimony, and martyrs arise to bear witness against their murderers.
